<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/troubleshooting-runbooks/allow-due-insufficient-app-data","lastmod":"2026-07-29T15:46Z","nid":"1539078"} -->
## Allow Due to Insufficient App Data

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/allow-due-insufficient-app-data
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Firewall Issues > Allow Due to Insufficient App Data
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:46Z
- Summary: This action is logged by the Service Edge when its Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) engine could not identify the network application. This typically happens when the connection gets terminated before enough packets can be processed to extract the required data.

This action is logged by the Service Edge when its Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) engine could not identify the network application. This typically happens when the connection gets terminated before enough packets can be processed to extract the required data.

The following describes how Zscaler Firewall uses DPI:

- The Zscaler Service Edge uses signature definitions to assign an application tree to each session, generally starting from the IP layer toward the Application layer (e.g., `ip.tcp.ssl.http2.office365.sharepoint_online` or `ip.tcp.ssl.https.wellsfargo`).
- Depending on the application's design and its signature's complexity, the information required to establish the complete application tree might not even be present in the first few packets. So, the Service Edge needs to allow and process the first few packets in each flow. Typically, this application tree is completed with the help of first 5 packets for common applications.
  - If the session is terminated by the client or the server before 12 packets, there are three different scenarios:
    - The Zscaler service could not even get one packet with data: DPI is not triggered, and the transaction is allowed or blocked depending on all the applicable firewall rules not containing network applications. Typically, 0.0.0.0 is logged as the Server Source IP for these entries because the server-side connection was never established.
    - **DPI has already built the app tree to the leaf application-layer node**: Transactions are allowed or blocked based on all the applicable firewall rules.
    - **DPI could not build the app tree**: All these packets (less than 12) are allowed, and the connection is logged as allowed due to insufficient app data in firewall insights. The topmost applicable firewall rule containing a network application is logged even though the application could not be identified. The action and the network application defined in the topmost applicable rule does not matter in this case because policy enforcement was postponed, but the other criteria must match. So it's possible that a block action is defined in the logged rule even though these packets were allowed for DPI while trying to identify the application defined in this rule. In the case of web traffic, all the Web Policy rules are first evaluated on the packets while waiting for DPI to complete the application tree. If there is a rule to block this transaction, then that policy is enforced. In this case, the reason **Blocked by Web Proxy Policy** is logged in firewall logs if the web filtering rules (Cloud App and URL Filtering) are configured to block this transaction.
  - If the session is terminated after 12 packets, there are two different scenarios:
    - DPI built the app tree, but stopped after the leaf application-layer node: This is the most common outcome. Transactions are allowed or blocked based on all the applicable firewall rules.
    - DPI failed to identify the application: This is very rare. DPI returns the application tree as ip.tcp.http, ip.tcp.ssl.https, or ip.udp.dns, based on the basic network information available in the first packet. If there's a firewall rule for these high-level network apps, those are evaluated and logged in the Firewall Insights logs. Otherwise, all the applicable firewall rules based on criteria other than network applications are evaluated. If the topmost matching rule contains a network application in its criteria, DPI influences policy enforcement and logging.
- During firewall policy enforcement, all the rules configured for all the network applications in the computed application tree are evaluated in a top-down manner. Here are some examples to illustrate how this works:
  - If you configure a rule at the top allowing an IP network application, all IP traffic is allowed regardless of any other TCP/UDP or more application-specific rules.
  - If the topmost rule blocks the HTTPS network service (e.g., TCP port 443) and the second rule allows the HTTPS network application, all port 443 traffic is blocked. The second rule is evaluated for HTTPS traffic on any other ports.

## Troubleshooting

To troubleshoot these issues:

1. Determine the firewall rule that should have matched and compare it with the criteria of the rule logged in the firewall logs.
2. Determine whether there are any rules containing TCP, UDP, or IP as network applications:
  - If not sure, you can search for TCP, UDP, and IP individually in the Firewall Control rules. This shows whether any of these are configured as Network Applications in any rules.
  - You must instead specify these as network services in the rule criteria if desired, because DPI is an overkill to identify whether a transaction makes use of TCP, UDP, or some other IP protocol.
3. Determine whether the rules containing network services are before the rules containing network applications:
  1. No or not sure:
    1. Look up the application name in the firewall rules. You can see all the rules containing that application as network service and network application.
    2. Additionally, go to **Administration**> **Resources**> **Network Services** and look up the port number for the right protocol. You might have configured the same port under two different network services. See image.
  2. The network service rule should ideally be placed before the network application rules wherever possible. This helps limit the scope of DPI to only the desired traffic.
  3. However, if you need to place a firewall rule with network application criteria near the top of the rule base, then you must define additional criteria to limit the scope of this rule only to the desired traffic.

## Solution

The following are solution steps:

1. If the network application is part of a higher-ordered rule, then blend the network application condition with at least one other condition that limits the rule to a very specific set of sessions/flows.
2. Attempt to order the rules with network applications lower than the rules without network applications. This not only allows for quicker policy enforcement for most traffic, but also reduces the number of flows for DPI to examime. An Advanced Firewall SKU is needed for enforcement of any rules configured with network applications. If you have recently downgraded from Advanced to Basic Firewall, you must clean up any such rules.

The following is an example of a poorly defined Firewall rule set to illustrate the solution:

1. Allow network application == SSH
2. Block network service == Telnet
3. Allow network service == HTTP, HTTPS, DNS
4. Block all (default cleanup/block rule)

It has two major problems:

- Rule 1 is too wide because it has no other criteria. All traffic passing through Zscaler Firewall is subject to DPI, and thus suffers delayed policy enforcement. The solution is to add more criteria (e.g., user, location, or network service) to limit the scope of this rule: With this rule set, DPI runs on all traffic from just this one user, thereby ensuring a quicker firewall policy enforcement for traffic from all the other users and locations.
  - Allow network application == SSH AND user == ceo@safemarch.net
  - Block network service == Telnet
  - Allow network service == HTTP, HTTPS, DNS
  - Block all (default cleanup/block rule)
- Because the network application rule is ranked first, Zscaler Firewall still examines every matching flow to identify the SSH application for this user's traffic. The application identification can take several packets on potentially many flows before DPI manages to deliver its verdict, as explained previously. The rule set proposed in the previous solution is still not optimally constructed, because rules 2 and 3 can be applied based on the first packets. Therefore, they should have been placed before the network application rule so that Zscaler Firewall could have immediately enforced those rules without having to wait for the DPI verdict. With this improved rule set, all TCP packets destined to the Telnet port are immediately blocked. All traffic to the HTTP, HTTPS, and DNS ports are also allowed. DPI is only required for traffic from all users and devices to SSH ports. If the SSH network application cannot be identified, the default rule blocks the connection.
  - Block network service == Telnet
  - Allow network service == HTTP, HTTPS, DNS
  - Allow network application == SSH AND network service == SSH
  - Block all (default cleanup/block rule)

If none of the above steps help, submit a case to [Zscaler Support](https://help.zscaler.com/contact-support) with the following information:

- A screenshot of the complete page at [https://ip.zscaler.com](https://ip.zscaler.com).
- If you have [enabled Remote Assistance](https://help.zscaler.com/unified/enabling-remote-assistance), the application name or FQDN, and the timestamp when a user tried accessing it via the Zscaler service. Otherwise, provide the Firewall Insights logs showing all the columns for the relevant transactions and a screenshot of the relevant rules showing all the criteria.

[Image: Port Protocol and Number]
<!-- /ZS-ARTICLE -->

---

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/troubleshooting-runbooks/block-policy-configured-access-gets-allowed","lastmod":"2026-07-29T15:38Z","nid":"1538981"} -->
## Block Policy Configured but Access Gets Allowed

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/block-policy-configured-access-gets-allowed
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Web Access Issues > Block Policy Configured but Access Gets Allowed
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:38Z
- Summary: This runbook articles describes how to determine and what steps to take when a block policy is configured but access is allowed anyway.

This runbook article describes how to determine that a block policy is configured but access is allowed anyway, and what steps to take.

## Review HTTP Headers

Review the HTTP headers to understand which URLs are allowed and what the response contains.

### Capture HTTP Headers

To learn more, see [How to Capture HTTP Headers (HAR file) on the Client System](https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-capture-http-headers-har-file-client-system).

### Analyze the HTTP Header Trace to Identify the Domains Used by the Website or Application

To learn more about analyzing the HTTP header trace to identify the domains used by the website or application, see [How to Analyze HTTP Headers](https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-analyze-http-headers).

## Review Web Insights Logs

Make sure that Web Insights logs show entries corresponding to the HTTP requests in the header trace and firewall insights show entries corresponding to the client PCAP. When traffic to the same domain gets intermittently allowed, it could be because those transactions do not even go to the Zscaler service.

If you do not see the traffic in the web logs, see the [Internet & SaaS Traffic Forwarding Troubleshooting Runbook](https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/zia-traffic-forwarding-troubleshooting-runbook).

Sometimes you can see entries in the web logs, but the column Bypassed Transaction shows **Yes**. This implies that the transaction did not go through the Zscaler service, but it was logged because you have enabled flow logging.

## Identify the Set of Polices Configured for the URL

Identify the set of policies configured for the URL categories and cloud applications you identified using the Web Insights logs.

- SSL Inspection Policy:
  - If the SSL Inspection rule is configured with the action **Do Not Inspect** and **Evaluate other policies**:
    - **URL Category limitation**: Only the domain part of the URL is used for policy evaluation.
    - **EUN behavior**: If **Show Notifications** for blocked traffic is enabled in this rule,
      - The Zscaler service must decrypt the transaction in order to display the End User Notification (EUN) in the user's browser. Generally in such cases, the Zscaler service doesn't connect to the remote server because the policy decision based on the request is to block the transaction.
      - The Zscaler service has access to more Layer 7 information in the web request due to this forced decryption, and then it may enforce an allow policy based on any additional criteria, if applicable. In that case, even though the Zscaler service initially decided to inspect the session only to show the block EUN, the transaction eventually is allowed without displaying any EUN.
  - Evaluating other policies only implies the URL and Cloud App Control policies. All the other policies require SSL Inspection.
- Cloud App Control:
  - If cascading isn't configured at the global or the rule level, then an explicit allow action in Cloud App Control bypasses the URL Filtering policy.
  - A Block in the Cloud App Control ends the policy evaluation, and URL Filtering or other policy rules aren't evaluated.
- URL Filtering: Review other criteria defined in the policy. Does the URL category value in the web logs match the expected category for this URL? You don't need to create a custom category for every URL that needs to be allowed. For example, if you want to allow a URL that is logged as **Professional Services** but gets blocked with the reason `Not allowed to browse this category`, you must first evaluate whether your business needs to block Professional Services for the given criteria. If your business requires blocking Professional Services for the concerned criteria, then you have to create a **Custom URL**category so that only a set of one or more URLs can be allowed while still blocking the parent category.
  - No: To learn more, see [How to Resolve User-Defined Category Conflicts](https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-resolve-user-defined-category-conflicts).
  - Yes: The rule ideally works as designed if the URL is correctly categorized. If you wish to choose a different action for this access using specific criteria, then create a rule above the applied rule with that action and more specific criteria.
- Does this concern a domain in the Miscellaneous URL Category?
  - Yes: Figure out whether the domain is added under a user-defined URL category.
    - As soon as you add a URL to a user-defined URL category, it gets removed from the **Miscellaneous**category by design.
    - Note that the **Miscellaneous**category is a catch-all category for the uncategorized URLs. In other words, for **Miscellaneous**or **Unknown URLs**, the behavior of the **URLs retaining parent** category and the **Keywords retaining parent** category is the same as **Custom URLs** and **Custom Keywords**, respectively.
    - **Solution**: If you want a specific uncategorized domain to match the policy for the **Miscellaneous**category, you must remove it from any custom categories. Otherwise, you must define a similar policy rule for the user-defined category.
  - Check whether [Suspicious New Domains Lookup](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-advanced-policy-settings#DomainLookup) is enabled under **URL & Cloud App Control**> **Advanced Policy Settings**. If enabled, then any **Newly Registered** or **Observed Domain** is also classified under the **Miscellaneous**category.
    - Review the [URL's category in Site Review](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/using-site-review-lookup-urls). If the **Current Categories**column shows the value **Newly Registered and Observed Domains**, it means the domain in question was either recently registered or observed; in both these cases, the Zscaler service considers a domain suspicious for 30 days after its detection.
    - Note that even if **Miscellaneous**doesn't show as the category, all these domains are also treated as Miscellaneous because they aren't classified under a specific predefined category.
    - If you have different policy rules for the **Miscellaneous**and **Newly Registered and Observed Domains** categories, then the rule at the top is enforced.
    - **Solution**: Either ensure that both rules have the same action, or move the rule with the desired action just above the other rule. For example, if you want to block the **Newly Registered and Observed Domains** category while allowing **Miscellaneous**, your block rule for the **Newly Registered and Observed Domains** category should be above the allow rule for the **Miscellaneous**category.
  - If [AI/ML-based Content Categorization](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-advanced-policy-settings#Dynamic) is enabled under **URL & Cloud App Control** > **Advanced Policy Settings**, then policy enforcement for SSL Inspected transactions to a URL in the **Miscellaneous**category is deferred until the Zscaler service receives the response from the server.
    - If the server does not respond or if the client terminates the connection due to a timeout while the server has yet to provide a complete response, this can lead to the policy not getting applied. In this case, the received bytes column in the web logs shows **0**.
    - **Solution**: There's no real issue here because the connection wasn't established between the client and the server because the client decided to terminate the connection. However, if a more consistent logging behavior is desired, you can disable AI/ML-based Content Categorization. This is a global change.
- Is the impacted user selected in the expected rule, or are they a member of one of the selected groups?
  - Review the user, group, and department values in the web logs. If the user field contains a special NoAuth user or the location name, it indicates an authentication failure or an authentication exemption. Note that rules with users, groups, or departments as criteria cannot be evaluated for such transactions.
  - Note down the users, groups, and departments configured as criteria in the expected rule.
  - Go to **User Management** and validate that the user is a member of one of the selected groups or departments.
- Does this concern only Connect requests or undecrypted SSL traffic from a known location?
  - Yes: If **Not Inspected** SSL connections don't match the policy, or if only Connect requests don't match the policy, but the subsequent HTTP requests are blocked or allowed as expected, this is likely by design.
    - If the domain is not configured to be bypassed by SSL inspection, look at the **SSL Policy Reason** field's value in the web logs and see the [SSL Policy Reason runbook](https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/ssl-policy-reason-runbook).
    - Is the concerned traffic coming from a location configured in the Admin Portal? If yes, review the concerned location's settings.
      - Policy is only enforced on the host part of the URL if **Enforce Authentication** is not enabled for the location.
      - Otherwise, the Connect transactions always show **Allowed**in the web logs. Zscaler Service Edge is designed to allow SSL handshake or Connect requests from all the locations where **Enforce Authentication** is enabled because it needs to obtain information of the authenticated user, which isn't visible in the Connect request or in the SSL handshake. This user information is critical for logging and enforcement of policies based on users and groups.
  - **Solution**: If SSL inspection is not desired for the traffic to a given domain, ensure that the SSL Inspection rule is configured with the action **Evaluate Other Policies**.
    - If this configuration isn't possible, then enable an IP surrogate on the location.
    - Alternatively, enable **Policy**for unauthenticated traffic from **Administration**> **Advanced Settings**
    - For more details, submit a case to [Zscaler Support](https://help.zscaler.com/contact-support).

## Review Firewall Logs

Review firewall logs with the filters for the Server Destination IP and the Client Source IP. Are there any logs?

- No: This traffic is likely not going via the Zscaler service. To learn more, see the [Internet & SaaS Traffic Forwarding Troubleshooting Runbook](https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/zia-traffic-forwarding-troubleshooting-runbook).
- Yes:
  - If any specific nonstandard ports are used for web traffic, you can configure them to be [processed as web traffic](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-advanced-settings#HTTP-Web-Proxy).
  - If this web traffic uses nonstandard ports that are dynamic in nature, i.e. the port number is not known or can change at runtime, then you can configure [Auto Proxy Forwarding](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-advanced-settings#auto-proxy-forwarding).

If none of these steps help, submit a case to [Zscaler Support](https://help.zscaler.com/contact-support) with the following information:

- A screenshot of the complete page at [https://ip.zscaler.com](https://ip.zscaler.com).
- If you [enable Remote Assistance](https://help.zscaler.com/unified/enabling-remote-assistance), the complete URL and the timestamp when a user tried accessing it via the Zscaler service. Otherwise, Web Insights logs showing all the columns for the relevant transactions and a screenshot of the relevant rule(s) showing all the criteria.
<!-- /ZS-ARTICLE -->

---

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/troubleshooting-runbooks/blocked-due-bad-ssl-record","lastmod":"2026-07-29T15:29Z","nid":"1538846"} -->
## Blocked Due to Bad SSL Record

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/blocked-due-bad-ssl-record
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > SSL Inspection Issues > Blocked Due to Bad SSL Record
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:29Z
- Summary: This article describes how to check why Internet & SaaS access policies deny a URL due to a bad SSL record.

In the following case, the SSL connection is blocked due to the forwarding of non-SSL traffic to the [ports configured for HTTPS Services](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-advanced-settings?referer=admin.zscaler.net#HTTP-Web-Proxy). This typically means either non-HTTP traffic encrypted using SSL or non-SSL traffic was sent to port 443.

Zscaler marks the transaction protocol as Tunnel SSL when some non-HTTP data is sent after an SSL handshake. The **Block Undecryptable Traffic** in the SSL Inspection Policy is used to control the policy behavior for such transactions.

In some scenarios, it's possible that the SSL handshake is successful, but then the application sends some non-HTTP data.

## Troubleshooting

1. You must collect packet captures on the client using Zscaler Client Connector, and then open the .pcap file using Wireshark.
2. If you see Data or HTTP or any other sections instead of Transport Layer Security (TLS) after Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) in the bottom pane, then it validates that non-TLS data was sent over this connection.
3. In the following image, you can see that the client initiates a connection on port 443 but then sends some other data instead of a Client Hello packet for TLS handshake. See image.
4. In a working scenario, you would always see a TLS section in the bottom pane. See image.

## Solution

The following are solution options:

- You can [configure a specific SSL Inspection Policy rule](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-SSL-inspection-policy) for the domain with the option “Block Undecryptable Traffic” disabled.
- If your business requires blocking all undecryptable traffic sent to HTTPS ports, you can configure an exemption for the affected domain using an SSL Inspection Policy rule with the action **Do Not Inspect**.
- If none of the above steps help, please submit a case to [Zscaler Support](https://help.zscaler.com/contact-support) with the following information:
  - If you [enabled Remote Assistance](https://help.zscaler.com/unified/enabling-remote-assistance), the URL and the timestamp when a user tried accessing the web application via Zscaler. Otherwise, the Web Insights logs showing all the columns for the relevant transactions.
  - Client packet capture (if [Zscaler Client Connector](https://help.zscaler.com/zscaler-client-connector/enabling-packet-capture-zscaler-client-connector) is installed).

[Image: Connection on Port 443]

[Image: Transport Layer Security (TLS)]

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/troubleshooting-runbooks/blocked-due-server-probe-failure","lastmod":"2026-07-29T15:28Z","nid":"1538943"} -->
## Blocked Due to Server Probe Failure

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/blocked-due-server-probe-failure
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Web Access Issues > Blocked Due to Server Probe Failure
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:28Z
- Summary: This runbook article describes if a policy action is triggered and the Zscaler Service Edge cannot make a successful TCP or TLS connection to the target web server. This happens when a web server either does not tolerate SSL Inspection or doesn't complete the TCP handshake with the ZZscaler Service Edge.

This runbook article describes how to resolve a triggered policy action when the Zscaler Service Edge cannot successfully connect to the target website that triggered the policy action via TCP or TLS. This happens when a web server either does not tolerate SSL Inspection or doesn't complete the TCP handshake with the Zscaler Service Edge.

## Troubleshooting

Verify that you can access the website from a test system with direct access to the internet. Validate the SSL configuration of the web server in question.

### Use an External Tool to Validate the Server's SSL Configuration

To learn more, see [How to Validate the SSL Configuration of a Web Server](https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-validate-ssl-configuration-web-server).

Review your organization's SSL Inspection policy for the concerned transactions.

If you have selected the action in the SSL Inspection policy as **Do Not Inspect** and **Evaluate Other Policies**, this error can still be displayed when the domain part of a URL is configured to be blocked in an access control policy, because the Zscaler service must decrypt a blocked transaction in order to show the**End User Notification**.

### Solution

The following items are possible solutions for the issue:

- If your business permits SSL Inspection for this domain, you can disable the option **Block Undecryptable Traffic** in the SSL Inspection rule for the domain with the action set to Inspect. To learn more, see [Configuring SSL Inspection Policy](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-SSL-inspection-policy).
- As a workaround, you can also set the action in the rule to **Do Not Inspect** and **Bypass Other Policies**.
- If none of these steps help, submit a case to [Zscaler Support](https://help.zscaler.com/contact-support) with the following information:
  - If you have [enabled **Remote Assistance**](https://help.zscaler.com/unified/enabling-remote-assistance), provide the complete URL in question, and the timestamp when a user tried accessing it via the Zscaler service. Otherwise, send the Web Insights logs showing all the columns for the relevant transactions.
  - If Zscaler Client Connector is installed, a client packet capture.
<!-- /ZS-ARTICLE -->

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/troubleshooting-runbooks/bypassed-due-missing-config","lastmod":"2026-07-29T15:45Z","nid":"1539088"} -->
## Bypassed Due to Missing Config

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/bypassed-due-missing-config
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Firewall Issues > Bypassed Due to Missing Config
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:45Z
- Summary: This action is logged in the rare circumstances when the Zscaler Service Edge fails to establish a connection with the Central Authority and consequently some traffic is allowed through Zscaler Firewall without policy enforcement.

This action is logged in the rare circumstances when the Public Service Edge fails to establish a connection with the Zscaler Central Authority (CA) and consequently some traffic is allowed through Zscaler Firewall without policy enforcement.

This typically only happens when traffic from a specific user or location arrives at the Service Edge for the first time and the Service Edge needs to download the policy config for that user or location, but the connection to the Zscaler Central Authority (CA) does not succeed due to problems outside Zscaler's network.

## Troubleshooting

How frequently is this value seen in your firewall logs for the past day or the past week?

1. Go to **Firewall Insights** > **Select Chart Type** as **Table** and **Units**as **Sessions**.
2. Note the number of sessions in **Overall Traffic** for the previous day or previous week. For the purposes of your calculations, this is called **TOTAL_SESSIONS**.
3. Go to **Firewall Logs** > **Apply**and usethe same time range as in the previous steps. Select the **Bypassed due to missing config in Action** filter. You can see the total count of sessions that were bypassed. For the purposes of your calculations, this is called **COUNT_BYPASSED**. If COUNT_BYPASSED is greater than 25K, you can try downloading this data to a CSV. If the COUNT_BYPASSED in the CSV is equal to 100,000, then you can either reduce the time period or look up these logs in your security information and event management (SIEM), if Nanolog Streaming Service (NSS) has been correctly deployed. To learn more, see [Understanding Nanolog Streaming Service](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/understanding-nanolog-streaming-service).
4. The percentage of bypassed transactions equals COUNT_BYPASSED x 100 divided by TOTAL_SESSIONS.

If the percentage of bypassed transactions is less than or equal to 0.05% of total sessions:

- This is the most general case. For instance, if the percentage of these bypassed sessions is 0.001% for a given day or week, it implies that the Zscaler service is correctly enforcing firewall policy for 99.999% of all the sessions for your organization.
- The Zscaler service provides a resilient cloud service that enables real-time policy enforcement on hundreds of nodes across the world, so it is bound to have small numbers of disconnections due to reasons outside its direct control. However, the Zscaler Engineering team is continuously working on further improving the resiliency of our configuration delivery mechanisms against these external factors.
- If you would like to have better control over the number of sessions that get bypassed due to missing config, see the Solutionsection.

If the percentage of bypassed transactions is more than 0.05% of total sessions, submit a case to [Zscaler Support](https://help.zscaler.com/contact-support). Enable [Remote Assistance](https://help.zscaler.com/unified/enabling-remote-assistance), or share the Firewall Insights logs showing all the columns for the policy action **Bypassed**due to missing configuration.

## Solution

The Zscaler Engineering team is working on providing a solution to control these transactions from your Zscaler Admin Console. However, if you'd like to change the policy behavior immediately, you can choose one of the following modes for this traffic and submit a case to [Zscaler Support](https://help.zscaler.com/contact-support) with the selected mode:

- Fail-Open Mode: This is the default mode. In this mode, if the Service Edge fails to establish a connection with the CA, the Service Edge bypasses policy evaluation for some transactions.
- Fail-Closed Mode: If your business prioritizes security over connectivity, a *fail-closed* mode can be configured. In this mode, the Service Edge blocks traffic by default and logs it in the Firewall Insights.
- Best Effort Policies: These policies provide an improved implementation of the fail-open mode. In this mode, the Service Edge applies a subset of Firewall rules defined in your Zscaler Admin Console. This subset includes:
  - All the rules without any user, group, or location criteria.
  - All the rules with user, group, or location criteria if this Service Edge had received traffic from those users, groups, or locations before the disconnection.
  - All the rules for the **Miscellaneous Unauthenticated Transactions** user (noauth-misc). To learn more, see [Configuring Policies for Unauthenticated Traffic](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-policies-for-unauthenticated-traffic).
<!-- /ZS-ARTICLE -->

---

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/troubleshooting-runbooks/cloud-app-block-action-configured-one-activity-all-activities-get-allowed-confirmed-web-logs","lastmod":"2026-07-29T15:36Z","nid":"1538970"} -->
## Cloud App: Block Action Is Configured for One Activity but All Activities Get Allowed as Confirmed by the Web Logs

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/cloud-app-block-action-configured-one-activity-all-activities-get-allowed-confirmed-web-logs
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Web Access Issues > Cloud App: Block Action Is Configured for One Activity but All Activities Get Allowed as Confirmed by the Web Logs
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:36Z
- Summary: This help article describes how to determine if a Block action is configured for one activity, but all activities get allowed as Confirmed by the Web logs.

This help article describes how to determine whether a Block action is configured for one activity, but all activities get allowed as Confirmed by the Web logs.

The first thing to do is find out which URLs are used when the user accesses the cloud app. Capture HTTP header traces while accessing the application. Note down the exact timestamps for specific activities such as upload, download, post, comment, like, etc.

The method to capture HTTP headers depends on how an end user accesses the website or the web application.

## The Website or Web Application Is Accessed from an Internet Browser

To learn more, see [How to Capture HTTP Headers (HAR file) on the Client System](https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-capture-http-headers-har-file-client-system).

## Make Sure No Transaction Uses QUIC

To learn more, see [How to Determine Whether a Website is Using QUIC](https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-determine-if-website-using-quic).

Look up the cloud app for a given URL either directly from the [Zscaler Admin Console](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/lookup-urls-admin-portal) or from the [Site Review Portal](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/using-site-review-lookup-urls).

## Troubleshooting

The following is a list of troubleshooting options:

- Review the HTTP header trace to figure out the key domains used at the timestamp corresponding to the activity of interest. For the remaining steps, consider the example of blocking upload, comment, or post activities, so you should look at all the POST requests to these domains.
- Make sure this traffic is SSL inspected. The **SSL Inspected** column in the web logs must show yes for the URL of interest. If the action in the relevant SSL Inspection rule for a cloud app is **Do Not Inspect & Evaluate Other Policies**, then only the domain part of the URL is available for policy enforcement, and the Zscaler service doesn't have access to sufficient data in order to differentiate between various activities such as upload or download.
- Have you ensured that the cloud app class and its name in the web logs match those defined in the policy and that the request method is POST?
  - Yes.
    - It's possible that the cloud application in question was very recently updated by its developers, which resulted in the signature becoming outdated for a specific activity within a specific cloud app.
    - Sometimes you can see that the Policy Action is Blocked and Allowed for the same request method, e.g. POST in this case, with the same cloud application; this happens when the app only changes its mechanisms for a set of activities such as liking or commenting.
    - Zscaler takes care of maintaining the most updated signatures of all cloud apps, which get released to the production clouds, following the [service update schedule](https://trust.zscaler.com/zscaler.net/maintenance) published on the Trust Portal. If there are any major changes in cloud app signatures, Zscaler also publishes a Trust notification with the appropriate information.
  - No
    - If the request method is not POST, then the Service Edge typically doesn't detect this activity as POST. Choose another activity applicable to this cloud app.
    - If the web logs show a different cloud app name, use that as criteria in the Cloud App rule.
- If none of the above steps help, submit a case to [Zscaler Support](https://help.zscaler.com/contact-support) with the following information:
  - If you have [enabled Remote Assistance](https://help.zscaler.com/unified/enabling-remote-assistance), the cloud app name or the URLs and the timestamp when a user tried accessing the application via the Zscaler service. Otherwise, Web Insights logs showing all the columns for the relevant transactions.
  - HTTP header trace from the end user's system while accessing the concerned cloud app.
  - Client packet capture (if [Zscaler Client Connector](https://help.zscaler.com/zscaler-client-connector/enabling-packet-capture-zscaler-client-connector) is installed).
<!-- /ZS-ARTICLE -->

## How to Analyze HTTP Headers

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-analyze-http-headers
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Debugging Tools > How to Analyze HTTP Headers
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:44Z
- Summary: Although most browsers allow exporting HTTP headers with or without data to a .har file, Fiddler typically saves them to a .saz file.

Although most browsers allow exporting HTTP headers with or without data to a `.har` file, Fiddler typically saves them to a `.saz` file.

## Approach 1

You can [install Fiddler from the official website](https://www.telerik.com/download/fiddler) and then import either the `.har` or the `.saz` file to review the HTTP headers.

If you do not want to install Fiddler, you can use one of the following approaches to analyze HAR files within a browser such as Google Chrome.

## Approach 2

You can import the HAR file directly in your browser developer tools as shown in the following image.

See image.

## Approach 3

You can use the [free web-based HAR analyzer tool in the Google Admin Toolbox](https://toolbox.googleapps.com/apps/har_analyzer/).

See image.

1. To review the HAR file in the Google HAR analyzer after the file is uploaded, review the list of the requests on the left, which can be filtered by code (e.g., 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, or via search). See image.
2. If you select a specific request, you can see details on the right:
  - The destination URL of the request.
  - The HTTP version.
    - This helps you determine whether the request is proxied through the Zscaler service (generally, the response is HTTP 1.1 unless the organization enabled and configured H2).
    - Alternatively, if you know H2 is configured for the domain, it can help confirm that HTTP2 is being used.
    - If this is Tunnel 1/Explicit Proxy, you can also look at the remote address to check whether it is a Proxy VIP.
  - Request method (GET, POST). For POST requests, you can see the request payload on the **Post Data** tab. For both GET and POST requests, you can view the response body on the**Response Content** tab.
  - The remote IP. This identifies which node a request is landing on. However, the Zscaler admin portals are now behind cloudfront CDN, so the IP is from AWS. See image.

[Image: The upload/import icon in the browser Developer Tools]

[Image: Google Toolbox]

[Image: Request List]

[Image: View the Web Request details]

## How to Capture HTTP Headers (HAR file) on the Client System

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-capture-http-headers-har-file-client-system
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Debugging Tools > How to Capture HTTP Headers (HAR file) on the Client System
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:44Z
- Summary: The method to capture HTTP headers depends on how an end user accesses the website or the web application.

The method to capture HTTP headers depends on how an end user accesses the website or the web application.

## The Website or Web Application Is Accessed from an Internet Browser

In this case, the most efficient method is to use the developer tools option available on most modern browsers.

Click one of the following options to read the relevant instructions:

- [Safari](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/capturing-http-headers-safari)
- [Mozilla Firefox](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/capturing-http-headers-mozilla-firefox)
- [Microsoft Edge](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/capturing-http-headers-microsoft-edge)
- [Google Chrome](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/capturing-http-headers-google-chrome)

The following sections provide detailed instructions on how to export complete HAR traces from latest Chromium-based browsers.

Chromium versions 130 and later limit the level of detail in the exported HAR file. For more information, refer to the [Google Release Notes](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-devtools-130#har). Although this level of detail is generally sufficient for most issues, you might want to capture all the HTTP data when debugging certain issues related to authentication or session-related errors, POST request failures, API debugging, or some complex interactions with third-party scripts or ads.

To capture all data in the exported HAR file, you must first adjust the settings in Developer Tools:

1. Click the **Settings**icon in the top right corner. See image.
2. Scroll down until you see the Network section and select the box **Allow to generate HAR (with sensitive data)**. See image.
3. Click and hold **Export** until a menu appears with the option to export sensitive data. See image.

### A Thick Application Is Required for Access

For such non-browser applications (e.g., Outlook, Teams, Slack), you need a third-party application such as Fiddler or Charles Proxy to capture the HTTP headers. These applications insert themselves as the system proxy to intercept and capture the web traffic.

Select one of the following options to read the relevant instructions for Fiddler.

### Zscaler Client Connector Is Not Enabled on the System

If Zscaler Client Connector is not enabled on the system:

1. Install Fiddler Classic. To perform a Fiddler capture, you must have Fiddler installed on the user machine. Download Fiddler Classic from the [official website](https://www.telerik.com/download/fiddler).
2. Launch Fiddler Classic. After Fiddler Classic is installed, launch it from the Start menu. See image.
3. Configure Fiddler Classic. Enable HTTPS decryption by going to **Tools**> **Options**> **HTTPS** and enabling the **Decrypt HTTPS traffic** checkbox. Click **Yes**to install and trust the Fiddler Classic Root certificate. See image.
4. Start the Fiddler capture. Click the **File**menu and ensure that the **Capture Traffic** option is enabled. See image.
5. Reproduce the problem. With Fiddler capturing the traffic, you can request the user to re-create the problem. At the same time, check whether Fiddler is capturing the live web traffic. See image.
6. Save the capture. Go to **File menu** > **Save**> **All sessions** to save the capture as `*.saz` file.

#### Zscaler Client Connector Is Enabled on the System

For instructions on what to do if Zscaler Client Connector is enabled on the system, see [Using Fiddler with Zscaler Client Connector](https://help.zscaler.com/zscaler-client-connector/using-fiddler-zscaler-app).

[Image: Capture Traffic]

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-determine-if-website-using-quic","lastmod":"2026-07-29T15:43Z","nid":"1539099"} -->
## How to Determine Whether a Website Is Using QUIC

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-determine-if-website-using-quic
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Debugging Tools > How to Determine Whether a Website Is Using QUIC
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:43Z
- Summary: You can use any of the following approaches to determine if a website is using QUIC: Browser Developer tools, Firewall Insights logs, and Client packet capture.

## Make Sure No Transaction Uses QUIC

Quick UDP Internet Connections (QUIC), also known as http/3 or h3, is a transport protocol developed by Google, designed to improve the performance of connection-oriented web applications. It operates over UDP instead of TCP and integrates features such as connection migration, multiplexing without head-of-line blocking, and built-in encryption (TLS 1.3).

For more information, see [Managing the QUIC Protocol](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/managing-quic-protocol).

You can use any of the following approaches to determine whether a website is using QUIC :

### Approach 1: Browser Developer Tools

This approach works for any websites or applications that allow access using a standard web browser such as Chrome, Firefox, Safari, etc. This example uses Google Chrome:

1. Open **Developer tools** in **Google Chrome**. Select the **Network**tab, and then right-click on one of the column titles. See image.
2. In this drop-down, ensure that **Protocol**is selected. You can see which HTTP protocol is used for each web request. Google Chrome shows QUIC as h3.
3. If you see a valid response code (such as 200) in the **Status**column for this h3 transaction, it implies that the concerned request was successful using QUIC.

If you want to know whether your browser and the network path are configured to allow QUIC, you can also use an external website such as https://quic.nginx.org/quic.html.

### Approach 2: Firewall Insights Logs

To view and configure the Firewall Insights logs:

1. Go to your Zscaler Admin Console.
2. Go to **Firewall Insights**and click the **Logs**tab. Verify that **Add the Network Service filter with QUIC** is selected. Add any additional filters such as client IP, username, location, etc. See image. The more filters you specify, the faster the query executes. But if your search query does not return any transactions, it's best to add filters gradually. For example, start with the most open filter, such as Network Service, and then if you see lots of transactions, add one more filter to get more specific search results.
3. If the first approach using HTTP header trace shows that the application or website used QUIC, but you don't see any entries in firewall logs for the time when the user tested this access, it indicates that the QUIC traffic did not go to the Zscaler service. To learn more, see the [Internet & SaaS Traffic Forwarding Troubleshooting Runbook](https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/zia-traffic-forwarding-troubleshooting-runbook).

### Approach 3: Client Packet Capture

To use a client packet capture to verify QUIC:

1. Close the **Concerned**tab in the web browser or the application.
2. If the end user has Zscaler Client Connector, use it to capture packets. Alternatively, install Wireshark and start a capture on all the interfaces.
3. After the capture is started, browse to the website or open the application. After browsing, stop the packet capture and open the file in Wireshark.
4. In Wireshark, use the display filter `quic and tls.handshake.type==1` to see all the SSL handshakes using QUIC. If there are no packets, either your capture was started after the website was already open or the website does not use QUIC.
5. Add a column for the SNI extension. See image.
6. Now you should be able to view all the server names with which QUIC was used for web traffic.

[Image: Network Tab]

[Image: Insights Logs]

[Image: SNI Extension]
<!-- /ZS-ARTICLE -->

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-resolve-user-defined-category-conflicts","lastmod":"2026-07-29T15:38Z","nid":"1539100"} -->
## How to Resolve User-Defined Category Conflicts

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-resolve-user-defined-category-conflicts
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Debugging Tools > How to Resolve User-Defined Category Conflicts
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:38Z
- Summary: Sometimes you might notice that you have configured a URL or a keyword under a specific category but the expected category does not show up in the Web Insights logs for the URL even though the URL matches.

Sometimes you might see that you have configured a URL or a keyword under a specific category, but the expected category does not show up in the Web Insights logs for the URL even though the URL matches.

To resolve such conflicts:

1. Review the **Categorization Method** and **URL Category** columns in the web logs of the concerned transactions. The Categorization Method column shows how the category was determined for the URL shown in the web log entry:
  - **Database A**: Indicates that the URL was categorized as per Zscaler's proprietary URL database.
  - **Database B**: Implies categorization based on a third-party vendor’s URL database.
  - **AI/ML-based content categorization**: Refers to the content classification of uncategorized pages using artificial intelligence (AI) or machine learning (ML).
  - **User-Defined**: Indicates that an administrator explicitly defined the category.
  - **None**: Indicates that the category of the URL is unavailable using any of the above methods.
2. If **Categorization Method** does not show **User-Defined**, review the **URL Category** to determine why the URL is not categorized under a user-defined category.
3. Go to [https://sitereview.zscaler.com](https://sitereview.zscaler.com) while your system is connected to Internet & SaaS (ZIA), and review all the predefined categories to which this URL or domain belongs. See image.
4. Search for this domain in the URL Categories defined under **Policies**> **Access Control**>**Internet & SaaS**>**URL Control**> **URL Categories**.
5. To find the categories containing the domain:
  - **Approach 1**: Edit one of the concerned URL categories and click the **Review Matches** drop-down menu. This option lets you view the matches and do the following:
    1. Add any overlapping domains from this category to any other matching category so that all these categories have the same URL entry.
    2. Add any overlapping domains from a matching URL category to the category that you're currently editing. See image.
  - **Approach 2**: Use the search bar at the top right of this page. For example, if you have added the URL `abc.def.xyz.com/query?path_value`, then you should search for the keyword `xyz`. See image.
6. Is this domain present in a user-defined category?
  - **No**. If you wish to add it to a custom category, follow the steps in [Configuring Custom URL Categories](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-custom-url-categories).
  - **Yes**. If the domain belongs to multiple categories, the effective URL categories are determined based on the following two factors:
    - Whether the URL is added to the **Custom URLs** field or the URLs retaining **Parent Category** field
      - If you add `drive.google.com` to the **Custom URLs** field in the category **CAT1**, then this domain no longer belongs to the predefined category **FileHost**for this customer. Any policy (not just **URL Filtering** but any other policy that uses URL category in the rule criteria) for the **FileHost**category doesn't apply on the transactions to this domain. This impact not only policy evaluation, but also reporting. For instance, if you add `.office365.com` to the **Custom URLs** field of a category **CAT1**, the O365 traffic might not show up in an Office365 report, and it could also lead to undesirable **SSL Inspection** policy enforcement.
      - It's recommended to add these URLs to the **Parent Category** field because this ensures that all the access control policy rules are enforced for the user-defined and the predefined categories based on Zscaler's **URL**categorization. It has no impact on any predefined reports and dashboards.
    - The most specific match:
      - In the following example, **CAT1**contains only `.google.com` in the **Custom URLs** field and **CAT2**contains only `drive.google.com` in the **Custom URLs** field.
        - If the user tries to access Google Drive (drive.google.com), only the policy for **CAT2**is enforced.
        - Even if no policy matches for the **CAT2**category, the policy for **CAT1**or the parent predefined category **FileHost**is not evaluated.
        - So, this transaction is implicitly allowed unless there's an explicit block or any rule at the bottom.
      - Taking a second example, **CAT3**contains `drive.google.com` and `.google.com` and **CAT4**contains `mail.google.com` and `.google.com`. All these URLs are added in the URLs retaining the **Parent Category** field.
        - If the user tries accessing Google Drive (drive.google.com), then only the policy for **CAT3**and **FileHost**match. Similarly for Gmail (mail.google.com), **CAT4**and **Webmail**are used for policy evaluation.
        - If the user tries accessing www.google.com, then the most specific match becomes `.google.com`, which is present in both **CAT3**and **CAT4**. So, all the rules for the **CAT3**, **CAT4**, and **WebSearch**are selected, and the topmost rule is enforced.
      - Using a third example, if you add `drive.google.com` directly to authentication exemptions and **CAT5**contains `.google.com` in the URLs retaining **Parent Category** field:
        - If the user tries accessing Google Drive (drive.google.com), only the policy for **FileHost**is matched, because the authentication exemption and the predefined category is the most specific match.
        - For all the other subdomains of .google.com, the policy for **CAT5**and the applicable predefined categories is evaluated.

#### Solution

When adding a specific subdomain to a Custom Category, add it to all the existing user-defined categories that contain the top-level domain unless you want to enforce the policy only on the most specific match. To learn more, see this [Zenith Community post](https://community.zscaler.com/Zenith/s/question/0D54u00009evn0dCAA/url-filtering-when-a-urldomain-is-present-in-multiple-custom-categories).

Sometimes, the correct category gets selected for policy enforcement, but a different category still gets logged in the web logs based on how the policy is configured for all the matching categories.

1. The Block action is configured according to the same rule for all the categories. The access is blocked, and no other rules are evaluated for this traffic.
2. The Block action is configured for at least one category and an Allow action for others. If the Block rule is above the Allow rule, access is blocked. Otherwise, access is allowed only by the URL Filtering policy, but the effective policy action will depend on the verdict of the remaining modules as shown in the following diagram. See image.
3. If you see an unexpected URL category value in the Web Insights logs, submit a case to [Zscaler Support](https://help.zscaler.com/contact-support) with the following information:
  - If you have [enabled Remote Assistance](https://help.zscaler.com/unified/enabling-remote-assistance), provide the complete URL and the timestamp when the user tried accessing it via the Zscaler service. Otherwise, include Web Insights logs showing all the columns for the relevant transactions.
  - A screenshot of the policy rule(s) that should have applied to these transactions.

## How to Test Whether a Website Works with the XFF Header

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-test-if-website-does-not-work-xff-header
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Debugging Tools > How to Test Whether a Website Works with the XFF Header
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:39Z
- Summary: X-Forwarded-For is an HTTP header. This header indicates to the destination web server that the web request is forwarded by a proxy on behalf of another IP. If the website is accessible only when SSL inspection is disabled, verify whether the website works well with the XFF header.

If the website is accessible only when SSL inspection is disabled, verify whether the website works well with the XFF header.

## What Is XFF?

X-Forwarded-For is an HTTP header. This header indicates to the destination web server that the web request is forwarded by a proxy on behalf of another IP. For example, if a web server receives traffic from the source IP 165.225.21.234 and this HTTP request contains the header X-Forwarded-For 88.127.24.87, the web server knows that 165.225.21.234 is likely a proxy and one of the hosts behind 88.127.24.87 generated the HTTP request.

Many websites extensively use this header. The most common example at Zscaler is [https://ip.zscaler.com](https://ip.zscaler.com), which shows both the proxy and the XFF IP.

Occasionally there might be some scenarios where Public Service Edge for Internet & SaaS (ZIA) receives web traffic from a downstream proxy. In such cases, the web request comes to the Zscaler service with the client's private IP in the XFF header. If you enable **Use XFF from Client Request**for such a location by logging in to Internet & SaaS and going to **Infrastructure**> **Locations**> **Location Management**, the Zscaler service used this private IP for detecting sublocations and logs it in the Client IP column in the web logs. The Service Edge removes any such XFF headers and replaces them with the XFF header containing the client's external IP before forwarding the request to destination server.

If you see **Not Inspected ...** in the **SSL Policy Reason** column, then the Zscaler cloud could not have inserted the XFF header in such transactions.

If SSL Inspection is enabled for a domain, the Zscaler service almost always inserts this XFF header in the web requests. Here are some exceptions:

If the domain falls under the Miscellaneous or Legal Liability categories, the Zscaler service does not insert XFF to prevent your egress IPs from getting denylisted. Here's a short explanation:

- If a domain is uncategorized (**Miscellaneous**), the Zscaler service's AI/ML-Based Content Classification Engine can dynamically determine its category based on the website's response content.
- If such a website is serving suspicious content, then the Zscaler service blocks the response.
- There are certain IP reputation vendors that monitor the XFF IP in the request to such domains. Now, even though the suspicious domain wasn't really accessed, your egress IP gets a bad reputation because we exposed it in the XFF header.
- If the transaction does not go through a Public Service Edge and the XFF insertion is disabled on the Virtual Service Edge. In this case, the `/sc/sme/conf/sc.conf` file contains the following line:

```
xff_enable=0
```

If the transaction is related to Source IP Anchoring and the option **Insert XFF Header for ZPA Traffic** under **Policies**>**Common Configuration**>**Advanced**>**Advanced Settings** is disabled, see [Configuring Advanced Settings](https://help.zscaler.com/zia/configuring-advanced-settings#xff-header-zpa-traffic).

There are some websites that do not return a valid response if they receive a web request containing the XFF header (e.g., agriculture.canada.ca, talabat.com).

- Here are some typical reasons: explicitly block all traffic coming from a proxy, absence of code in the web server to process this header, improper implementation of redirects or response codes.
- Some of these websites return an error code, and some others might time out, but they almost never explicitly state in the error code that the request was not successful because it contained an XFF header.

## Troubleshooting

Here's how you can test the compatibility with the XFF header for any website on a test laptop that has direct internet access:

- On Google Chrome:
  1. If it isn't already installed, install the free ModHeader extension from Google Chrome Web Store. See image.
  2. Select the extension from the top right. See image.
  3. Then enter in the name of the XFF header and enter a valid IP value. (Here an invalid value 2000.2000.2000.2000 is shown just to emphasize that this IP is not used for routing.) See image.
  4. Make sure that the top bar shows the pause button, which implies that this extension is already inserting this header in all the outgoing web requests from all the tabs of this browser.
  5. Now you can first test that the header insertion is successful by going to https://ip.zscaler.com and ensure that the traffic is not going through the Zscaler service.
  6. You can now try to access the website with and without the XFF header on this system.
- On Mozilla Firefox:
  1. If it isn't already installed, install the free Modify Header Value extension from the Firefox extensions store. See image.
  2. Turn off Internet & SaaS in your Zscaler Client Connector.
  3. Open the extension from the top right. See image.
  4. Specify the URL, XFF, and the IP value as shown below. Then click on **Add**. An ACTIVE rule appears at the bottom. See image.
  5. You can use this toggle in the option to enable or disable the insertion of XFF header. See image.
  6. Test that the header insertion is successful by going to https://ip.zscaler.com and ensure that the traffic is not going through the Zscaler service.
  7. Try to access the website with and without the XFF header on this system.

## Solution

Because XFF is a standard header, most web applications should fix their logic to support it in the HTTP requests. To fix HTTP requests to be XFF compliant, reach out to the web development team managing the website.

- If the website is trusted and your business policy allows disabling SSL inspection for this domain, then turning off SSL Inspection automatically disables insertion of XFF.
- If none of the above solutions work, submit a case to [Zscaler Support](https://help.zscaler.com/contact-support).

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-validate-ssl-configuration-web-server","lastmod":"2026-07-29T15:31Z","nid":"1539104"} -->
## How to Validate the SSL Configuration of a Web Server

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/troubleshooting-runbooks/how-validate-ssl-configuration-web-server
- Product: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks
- Path: Zscaler Support Troubleshooting Runbooks > Internet & SaaS Access Control Policies Troubleshooting Runbook > Debugging Tools > How to Validate the SSL Configuration of a Web Server
- Last modified: 2026-07-29T15:31Z
- Summary: This runbook article describes how to validate the SSL configuration of a web server.

When the Internet & SaaS (ZIA) Public Service Edge either cannot complete the handshake with a web server or detects the certificate as untrusted or bad, it's best to cross-validate certain attributes of the public website's SSL configuration.

- Which attributes should I validate?
  - Does the server offer strong cipher suites?
  - Does the requested SNI match the Common Name (CN) or Subject Alternative Names (SAN) values in the certificate?
  - Is the server certificate expired or revoked?
  - Does the server offer the complete, unbroken certificate chain all the way up to a root CA?
  - Is the issuer root certificate trusted by most modern browsers?
  - Does the server support strong key exchange algorithms?
- [https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/](https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/)
  - This free website performs a deep analysis of the configuration of any SSL web server on the public Internet. This includes all of the above certificate information in more detail along with SSL configuration on the web server, including the supported protocols and cipher suites. It also has standard automated tests for different platforms to show whether a website is compatible with various client or browser versions.
  - Enter the website's FQDN.
  - Look at the summary indicators for Certificate, Protocol Support, Key Exchange and Cipher Strength. If any of these is not green, it helps explain why this certificate was considered bad or untrusted.
  - The last three indicators are calculated based on the server’s SSL configuration and are independent of the server’s certificate.
- [https://aboutssl.org/ssl-tools/ssl-checker.php](https://aboutssl.org/ssl-tools/ssl-checker.php)
  - This free website performs a basic analysis of the certificate of any SSL web server on the public Internet.
  - Do most modern browsers trust this certificate?
  - When does the certificate expire?
  - Is the server hostname listed in the certificate?
  - The website shows the complete certificate chain with main attributes of each certification, including Common Name (CN), SAN, validity, Serial Number, Issuer, and signature algorithm.
- [https://badssl.com/](https://badssl.com/)
  - This website provides a variety of deliberately broken SSL configurations to help test the client applications, browsers, and tools against different types of SSL/TLS issues.
  - On this website, users can see how their software handles various SSL/TLS problems, such as expired certificates, weak ciphers, and incorrect hostname configurations. This testing helps ensure that applications properly handle SSL/TLS errors and maintain robust security practices.
- [https://decoder.link/ocsp](https://decoder.link/ocsp)
  - Submit Base64-encoded CSR or certificate to query the corresponding OCSP response and view the revocation status.
- Command-line `openssl` utility All these commands are shown with the domain example.com, which you must replace with the server that you wish to test.
  - Verify the **Protocol Version Support**. Run the following commands in a shell: `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_3 2>&1 | grep "Protocol"``echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_2 2>&1 | grep "Protocol"``echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1 2>&1`If you see **Protocol: TLSv1.2** or **Protocol: TLSv1.2** in the output, it indicates that the server supports those protocols. And for tls1 or ssl3, you should ideally see an error message indicating handshake failure or connection timeout.
  - Verify Cipher Strength:
    1. Print the preferred default cipher suite used by a given domain: `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>&1 | grep "Cipher is"`The output must be similar to: **Cipher is ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384** Strong ciphers typically include ECDHE/DHE for perfect forward secrecy, AES-256/AES-128 for encryption algorithm, GCM/CBC for encryption mode and SHA256/SHA384 for hashing.
    2. Conversely, you can check for weak cipher support using the following commands: `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -cipher 'RC4' 2>&1``echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -cipher '3DES' 2>&1``echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -cipher 'MD5' 2>&1`The output should show handshake failure or no cipher match if the server properly rejects weak ciphers. If you see the Cipher is RC4-SHA or similar, the server accepts weak ciphers.
  - Validate that the FQDN in the URL matches the CN or SAN in the certificate:
    1. Initiate an SSL handshake for a specific FQDN using the servername option: `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername www.example.com 2>&1`
    2. Print the CN in the server certificate, which must match the requested FQDN: `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername www.example.com 2>&1 | openssl x509 -noout -subject`
    3. If the CN doesn't match, print SAN, one of which must match the FQDN: `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername www.example.com 2>&1 | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep -A1 "Subject Alternative Name"`
  - Validate that the certificate is not expired or self-signed:
    1. Print the **notBefore**and **notAfter**dates of the server certificate: `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>&1 | openssl x509 -noout -dates`Ensure that the current time is between the **notBefore**and **notAfter**values.
    2. Print the **Issuer**and **Subject**values from the certificate: `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>&1 | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer`If the **Issuer**and **Subject**values are identical, then the certificate is self-signed. This must never be seen for a public website in production.
  - Validate that the certificate chain is complete to the root certificate:
    1. Show the count of number of certificates returned by a server: `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts 2>&1 | grep -c "BEGIN CERTIFICATE"`If the output is **1**, then there is really no chain and the Issuer in the only certificate must be present in the Trusted CA store used by the application.
    2. If there are two or more certificates in the chain, print the **Subject Key Identifier** and **Authority Key Identifier** of each certificate in the chain: `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts 2>&1 | awk -F'\n' 'BEGIN { showcert = "openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectKeyIdentifier,authorityKeyIdentifier" } /-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----/ {printf "\nCertificate %d: \n", i} {printf $0"\n" | showcert} /-----END CERTIFICATE-----/ {close(showcert) i++}' 2>/dev/null`If the certificate chain is complete, then AKI of Certificate 0 must match SKI of Certificate 1, AKI of Certificate 1 must match SKI of Certificate 2, and so on.
  - Validate that the certificate is not revoked:
    1. Extract the **OCSP URL** from the certificate: `echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername www.example.com 2>&1 | openssl x509 -noout -ocsp_uri`The output must show the **OCSP URL** if that extension is attached by the server (e.g., `http://ocsp.digicert.com`).
    2. Download the leaf certificate and the remaining certificate chain to separate files: `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>&1 < /dev/null | sed -n '/-----BEGIN/,/-----END/p' > leaf.pem``echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts 2>/dev/null | sed -e '1,/-----END CERTIFICATE-----/d' > chain.pem`
    3. Fetch the **OCSP**result from the **OCSP URL** for the given certificate: `openssl ocsp -issuer root.pem -cert example.pem -resp_text -noverify -url http://ocsp.digicert.com | grep -A2 "Cert Status"`
<!-- /ZS-ARTICLE -->
